findings.headline: Significant concentration of borrowing due within 12 months requires refinancing
findings.detail: The council has 25% of £144m borrowing (approximately £36m) maturing within 12 months. While within policy limits (50% upper), this represents substantial refinancing requirement at time when treasury advisors forecast rates unchanged but markets are pricing in potential increases.
findings.matters: Concentration of near-term maturities creates refinancing risk; if rates rise while the council refinances £36m, borrowing costs could increase materially from the current 2.87% average.
findings.figures: £144m total borrowing; 25% due within 12 months; current average interest rate 2.87%
findings.quote: Under 12 months 50% 0% 25%

findings.headline: Council relying on one-time PWLB early redemption discount to boost reserves
findings.detail: The council received a £14.6m discount from early repayment of a 50-year PWLB loan, being amortised over 10 years and used to increase the Interest Rate Equalisation reserve. This is a non-recurring gain that will not support future budgets once amortisation ends.
findings.matters: Using a non-recurring windfall to boost reserves creates false impression of financial strength and makes budget balancing more difficult in future years.
findings.figures: £14.6m discount from early PWLB repayment amortised over 10 years
findings.quote: Following the early repayment of a 50-year PWLB loan, a discount was received. The discount is to be amortised over 10 years

findings.headline: Crown House loan revalued downward due to non-market interest rate
findings.detail: The council holds £57.8m in loans to subsidiary companies (Graven Hill and Crown House) as non-treasury investments. The Crown House loan, at a non-market interest rate, has been discounted using a 5% effective rate for IFRS9 accounting purposes, indicating the actual value is lower than the cash advanced.
findings.matters: Loans at non-market rates suggest capital misallocation or subsidies; the IFRS9 revaluation indicates overvaluation of the investment or risk in the underlying company.
findings.figures: £57.8m loans to subsidiaries; £102.9m total non-treasury investments; Crown House loan discounted using 5% effective rate
findings.quote: The loan is at a non-market rate of interest and has therefore been discounted using an effective interest rate of 5%, which the directors consider to be an appropriate market rate.

findings.headline: Council using one-off treasury surplus to offset service budget overspends
findings.detail: The council generated a £1.078m treasury management surplus during 2025-26 which is being used to offset service overspends rather than retained as reserve. This indicates the underlying service budget was under pressure and the council relied on investment income to balance. While total treasury performance was strong (£1.957m also transferred to reserves), using gains to cover current overspends is not sustainable.
findings.matters: Reliance on one-off treasury gains to cover recurring service overspends signals underlying budget stress; it indicates difficulty balancing future budgets without continued strong investment performance.
findings.figures: £1.078m surplus offsetting service overspends; £1.957m transferred to Interest Rate Equalisation reserve
findings.quote: the (£1.078m) surplus is being used to offset service overspends

findings.detail: The workforce strategy risk notes indications that specific service areas continue to experience recruitment difficulties for professional roles. findings.detail: The register identifies a significant risk around failure to properly manage Oxfordshire Housing and Growth Deal infrastructure projects being delivered by Oxfordshire County Council. This could lead to HM Government holding back or requiring repayment of funding if the council fails to meet timely obligations.

findings.detail: The leadership risk register identifies that work is underway with one company to establish long-term support arrangements. This is explicitly listed in mitigating actions for the sustainability of council owned companies risk. The council holds regular Shareholder meetings and quarterly Shareholder Liaison Meetings to monitor performance.
findings.matters: Council-owned company performance directly affects the council's balance sheet and financial sustainability
findings.figures: none

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 - Leadership Risk Register as at 17/04/2026
findings.headline: Council agreed 2026/27 budget with savings proposals but requires monitoring for slippage
findings.detail: The council has agreed a budget for 2026/27 with identified savings proposals to address reductions in funding. The register emphasizes that close monitoring of the savings programme delivery will be required throughout the year, with mitigations needed if slippage occurs. Additionally, consultation on treatment of Pooling payments is expected in 2026, which could affect funding further.
findings.matters: Lenders need to know whether the council can execute planned savings in the face of funding reductions
findings.figures: none
findings.quote: The budget for 2026/27 was agreed with savings proposals identified to contribute to addressing reductions in funding. Close monitoring of the delivery of the savings programme will take place throughout 2026/27 with mitigations required if slippage is identified.

findings.headline: £0.335m of the £1.518m total savings (22%) comes from balance sheet management, not operational efficiency
findings.detail: The single largest savings item is a balance sheet review where the council used available resources to lower borrowing costs. This represents nearly a quarter of the total claimed savings and is a non-recurring reserve withdrawal, not an operational saving.
findings.matters: Drawing on reserves to meet financial targets rather than achieving sustainable operational improvements raises questions about underlying budget sustainability
findings.figures: £0.335m out of £1.518m total savings
findings.quote: After reviewing our balance sheet, using available resources to help lower borrowing costs (0.335) Achieved

findings.headline: Overtime policy changes totalling £0.081m were explicitly decided not to proceed with
findings.detail: The council planned to save £0.040m (environmental) and £0.041m (HR) by reducing weekday overtime rates to standard pay, but made a deliberate decision not to implement the Overtime Policy change. This indicates the council faced constraints preventing the saving.
findings.matters: Indicates cost pressures around employment and wages that the council could not or chose not to address through policy
findings.figures: £0.081m total (£0.040m environmental + £0.041m HR)
findings.quote: The saving was not achieved due to the decision to not implement the change in the Overtime Policy

findings.headline: Car parking revenue declined rather than increasing, recording -£0.071m against a £0.100m savings target
findings.detail: The council planned to save £0.100m by raising car park charges but instead saw parking income fall, achieving -£0.071m. This shortfall reflects reduced footfall in town centres, which the council describes as a national trend. The net effect is a £0.171m swing against plan.
findings.matters: Signals underlying weakness in town centre activity and consumer demand; shows price elasticity working against revenue forecasts
findings.figures: Target £0.100m savings; actual outcome -£0.071m
findings.quote: The anticipated savings in parking were only partially achieved (-0.071) because of reduced car parking income. The reduction in car parking income reflects reduced footfall in town centres. This is reflective of national trends.

findings.headline: Leisure contracts saving of £0.350m not delivered due to delayed Parkwood Agency contract implementation
findings.detail: The council planned to save £0.350m through reducing costs in leisure contracts via the Parkwood Agency contract but did not achieve this in 2025-26 due to delayed implementation. At £0.350m, this is the largest single saving missed in the plan.
findings.matters: Large operational savings not materialising signals execution risk on cost control and reliability of future budget forecasts
findings.quote: The saving was not achieved due to delayed implementation of the Parkwood Agency contract.

findings.headline: Below-market interest rate loan to subsidiary Crown House Banbury required £9.5 million accounting adjustment
findings.detail: The Council reduced the interest rate on its loan to subsidiary Crown House Banbury and had to account for the below-market-rate element separately, resulting in a £9.5 million reclassification between long-term investments and long-term debtors in the financial statements.
findings.matters: This adjustment suggests the council is subsidising its subsidiary at below-market rates, which affects both the true cost of the investment and the council's effective financial position.
findings.figures: £9.5m adjustment between long-term investments and long-term debtors
findings.quote: The Council have reduced the interest rate on the loan to its subsidiary, Crown House Banbury. The Council needed to account for the below market rate element on the loan separately. This resulted in an amendment of £9.5m between long term investments and long term debtors in the financial statement.

findings.headline: Planned savings of £1.807 million in 2024/25 missed by £0.629 million, increasing future year pressure
findings.detail: The Council failed to deliver £0.629m of its planned £1.807m savings in 2024/25. Although this was offset by underspends in base budgets for the current year, the shortfall increases pressure on future years and exacerbates the funding challenges outlined in the MTFS.
findings.matters: A lender assesses whether councils can deliver on their stated efficiency plans. Persistent savings shortfalls suggest the council may struggle to close the projected funding gaps.
findings.figures: £1.807m planned, £0.629m shortfall, £1.375m planned for 2025/26
findings.quote: In its Finance and Performance Monitoring end of year report, the Council recorded a shortfall in the delivery of planned savings amounting to £0.629 million for 2024/25. Notably, this non-delivery did not adversely affect the overall outturn position, as underspends in base budgets were sufficient to offset the shortfall. However, the failure to realise ongoing savings increases pressure on future years and may exacerbate the funding challenges outlined in the Medium-Term Financial Strategy.

findings.headline: Cumulative funding gap of £16.370 million across the medium-term financial strategy period
findings.detail: The Council faces annual shortfalls: £6.909m (2025/26), £4.946m (2026/27), £5.162m (2027/28), and £5.325m (2028/29). The council projects it will have sufficient reserves to offset these deficits, but is relying on future efficiency opportunities of £5.67m being developed.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand whether the council has a sustainable funding strategy beyond reserve drawdown for multi-year deficits.
findings.quote: When the budget for 2025/26 was set in February 2025, the MTFS was updated to reflect revised funding gaps of £4.946 million in 2026/27, £5.162 million in 2027/28, £5.325 million in 2028/29, and £0.937 million in 2029/30. The cumulative funding gap for this updated period stands at £16.370 million.

findings.paper_title: Budget & Corporate Plan Report 2026-27 to Council
findings.headline: The council's three-year funding settlement ends in 2028-29, with £8.5m of transitional protection at risk and no certainty of continuation.
findings.detail: The government has provided a three-year settlement running to 2028-29, which the council describes as its first multi-year settlement in a decade. However, 'In 2028/29 the council will be in receipt of £8.471m transitional protection. This is the last year of the Spending Review Period and there is no certainty of funding thereafter.' The council has developed alternative scenarios for what happens after 2028-29, including a 'phased reduction of transitional protection payments' and a potential 95% funding floor, but states these are scenarios for planning, not confirmed policy.
findings.matters: Beyond the three-year settlement, the council faces significant funding uncertainty. The removal of £8.5m in transitional protection in 2029-30 would create a substantial cliff-edge. The council's long-term solvency is dependent on further government transitional protections being put in place, which is not guaranteed.
findings.figures: £8.471m transitional protection in 2028-29; no certainty of funding beyond that point
findings.quote: This is the last year of the Spending Review Period and there is no certainty of funding thereafter.

findings.paper_title: Budget & Corporate Plan Report 2026-27 to Council
findings.headline: The council is drawing down reserves to fund the budget, with net use of £3.5m from revenue reserves in 2026-27.
findings.detail: Table 4.4.1 shows that revenue reserves will fall by a net £3.502m in 2026-27 (£3.835m use of earmarked reserves minus £0.333m receipt of revenue grants). Earmarked reserves are forecast to fall from £32.520m to £28.685m, and the council notes that 'Reserves can be used for one-off expenditure but should not be used to finance ongoing council activities.' Yet the use of reserves is being employed to manage the medium-term funding gap (Section 4.6.21): 'the council could consider making reserves available on a short-term basis' if savings delivery is delayed.
findings.matters: The council is using non-recurring resources to fund the budget. Reserves are declining across the forecast period, reducing the council's financial cushion. If reserves are depleted and savings do not materialise, the council will have limited options.
findings.figures: Net use of revenue reserves £3.502m in 2026-27; earmarked reserves forecast to fall to £28.685m by end of year
findings.quote: Reserves can be used for one-off expenditure but should not be used to finance ongoing council activities.

findings.paper_title: Budget & Corporate Plan Report 2026-27 to Council
findings.headline: Financing costs are 28.3% of the net revenue budget, and the council's capital leverage is rising.
findings.detail: Interest payable and MRP (principal repayment of borrowed capital) account for £9.1m out of the £32.3m net revenue budget (28.3%). The Capital Financing Requirement has risen to 84% of the book value of the council's long-term assets as of 31 March 2025, up from 81% in 2024-25. The council notes that 'it is important to continue to monitor the CFR to long-term asset ratio to consider appropriate next steps if the council's need to borrow (CFR) exceeds the total value of its capital assets'. The council has also set aside an 'interest rate risk reserve' because 'if interest rates do not fall in line with forecasts...then it has set aside an interest rate risk reserve as a further mitigation'.
findings.matters: The council's debt burden is significant and rising as a proportion of its assets. Nearly a third of gross revenue funding goes to servicing debt. Interest rate assumptions are critical to affordability, and the council is preparing for the risk that rates don't fall as forecast. This constrains future borrowing capacity and leaves the council exposed to interest rate volatility.
findings.figures: Financing costs £9.1m out of £32.3m net revenue budget (28.3%); CFR 84% of long-term assets
findings.quote: Budgeted interest and MRP represents 28.3 percent of the £32.3m net council Funding for 2026/27... if interest rates do not fall in line with the forecasts provided by the council's treasury advisor, then it has set aside an interest rate risk reserve as a further mitigation.

findings.paper_title: Budget & Corporate Plan Report 2026-27 to Council
findings.headline: Castle Quay regeneration income has been revised down by £1.1m due to economic headwinds and lease renewal uncertainty.
findings.detail: The 2026-27 budget reflects a downward revision of £1.131m in the forecast income from Castle Quay, the major regeneration project that is 'part of a long-term wider Banbury regeneration project'. The revision reflects 'the post pandemic economic climate', 'changes to the retail market and ongoing shopping patterns', and 'anticipated changes in rental agreements'. The council has made 'prudent assumptions about lease renewals within the current economic climate' and has explicitly not factored in potential benefits from increased footfall.
findings.matters: A material income stream from what the council describes as a strategic regeneration project has become less certain. Retail and hospitality remain weak, and the council is being cautious about lease renewals, suggesting commercial pressure on the properties held.
findings.figures: £1.131m downward revision to 2026-27 forecast compared to 2025-26 MTFS assumptions
findings.quote: The latest MTFS forecast takes into consideration: The current outturn forecasts for 2025/26; The post pandemic economic climate; Changes to the retail market and ongoing shopping patterns; Anticipated changes in rental agreements based on information available at the time of setting the budget.

findings.paper_title: Budget & Corporate Plan Report 2026-27 to Council
findings.headline: The council is counting on £3-4m of annual savings from a transformation programme that has not yet received formal approval.
findings.detail: The Cherwell Futures programme is expected to deliver £3-4m of annual ongoing savings, but the council explicitly states 'Until the formal business cases have been approved, none of these savings are assumed within the current MTFS'. An earmarked reserve of £1.1m has been set aside to fund the transformation work. The council has already identified that previous-year savings proposals 'have not been fully delivered', showing execution risk on its savings programmes.
findings.matters: The MTFS gap of £3m across the forecast period and the ability to address the 2027-28 cliff-edge depend on transformation savings that may not materialise. No business cases have been approved. If Cherwell Futures does not deliver, the council will need to find savings from elsewhere or use reserves, reducing financial flexibility.
findings.figures: £3-4m provisionally anticipated annual savings; £1.1m earmarked reserve for transformation
findings.quote: Provisionally, £3-4m of annual ongoing savings are anticipated from the current Cherwell Futures programme. Until the formal business cases have been approved, none of these savings are assumed within the current MTFS.

findings.paper_title: Budget & Corporate Plan Report 2026-27 to Council
findings.headline: Government changed the business rates pooling calculation after consultation, reducing the council's medium-term improvement from £4.4m to £2.1m.
findings.detail: The council had planned on the basis of provisional government guidance, expecting a £4.4m improvement from changes to business rates pooling treatment. When the final settlement was announced on 9 February 2026, the government changed the methodology for calculating pooling income, cutting the expected benefit by nearly half to £2.1m. The council explicitly states this 'severely impacted the council's medium term financial strategy', and it has set aside the one-off Adjustment Support Grant to absorb this shock.
findings.matters: The council's external funding has become less predictable. Government policy changes between provisional and final settlement created a £2.3m negative surprise. This shows reliance on government funding decisions that can shift, with limited notice.
findings.figures: Expected £4.4m improvement reduced to £2.1m; difference of £2.3m
findings.quote: However, the final settlement announced on 9 February 2026 contained materially different funding figures from 2027/28 onwards due to a significant change in the methodology to calculate pooling income. These reduced a £4.4m improvement to £2.1m and have severely impacted the council's medium term financial strategy.

findings.paper_title: Budget & Corporate Plan Report 2026-27 to Council
findings.headline: A £2.3m one-off government grant masks a structural funding deficit that will reappear in 2027-28.
findings.detail: The final government settlement announced on 9 February 2026 included a one-off Adjustment Support Grant of £2.335m to Cherwell for 2026-27, which covers the exact gap that will emerge in 2027-28 when it drops out. The council's MTFS (Table 4.6.2) shows a £2.335m funding gap in 2027-28, with the grant specified as covering 'a late shift from 100% to 50% business rates pooling benefit'. Without the grant, the council would run a deficit in 2026-27.
findings.matters: The council's balance in 2026-27 depends entirely on a non-recurring grant. A lender assessing the council's structural financial position needs to understand that 2026-27 is not a sustainable budget without this one-off support, and that a material funding pressure emerges immediately in 2027-28.
findings.figures: £2.335m Adjustment Support Grant in 2026/27; £2.335m funding gap in 2027/28
findings.quote: The impact on the baseline position is £2.335m, which will be mitigated in 2026/27 by the one-off Adjustment Support Grant, but which will result in an ongoing pressure from 2027/28.

findings.headline: Projects reserve completely depleted to zero by April 2026 after S151 review adds £3.46m
findings.detail: The Projects reserve opened at £5.61m, received £2.15m in transfers during 2025/26, and the S151 officer added a further £3.46m, bringing it to exactly £0.00 by April 2026. This means all project commitments are now accounted for and funded. No project contingency remains.
findings.matters: Once a projects reserve is depleted, any cost overruns on capital schemes or new project needs must be funded from general balances or additional borrowing. Lenders need to know how the council will absorb project pressures.
findings.figures: Projects Reserve: £5.610m (April 2025), 2.149 transfer, 3.461 S151 review, £0.000 (April 2026), £0.00 (end of period)
findings.quote: Projects Reserve: (5.610) opening, 2.149 transfer, 3.461 S151 review, 0.000 forecast closing balance, -  (all zeros) thereafter

findings.headline: Transformation implementation reserve of £6.24m shows major organisational change programme
findings.detail: A new Transformation implementation reserve is being created at £6.24m (£4.97m opening plus £1.26m transfer in 2025/26), with no planned draw over the forecast period. This signals the council has committed to a substantial transformation or restructuring programme funded from reserves.
findings.matters: Large transformation programmes carry execution risk and can distract senior management. A lender should understand the scope (redundancy, systems, structural) and whether the reserve is adequately funded or whether mid-programme additional funding might be needed.
findings.figures: Transformation implementation Reserve: £4.974m opening, (1.262) transfer, £6.236m forecast balance 1 April 2026, £0 balance by 2031
findings.quote: Transformation implementation Reserve: (4.974) opening, (1.262) transfer 2025/26, (6.236) forecast closing balance, no transfers 2026/27–2030/31

findings.headline: Legal Project reserve has been doubled in value, signalling anticipated legal or compliance costs
findings.detail: The Legal Project Reserve is being increased from £0.50m to £1.00m as a result of the S151 officer's review. This reserve exists to fund legal disputes or compliance work. The doubling suggests the finance officer has identified material legal costs ahead, likely relating to significant transactions or governance issues.
findings.matters: Unexpected legal costs can be material and distract finance teams. A lender should know whether the council is facing disputes (planning, employment, contract) that could affect deliverability or cash flow.
findings.figures: Legal Project Reserve: £0.500m (April 2025), (0.500) S151 review, £1.000m (April 2026 forecast), maintained at £1.000m thereafter
findings.quote: Legal Project Reserve: (0.500) opening, (0.500) S151 review, (1.000) forecast balance 1 April 2026

findings.headline: Business rates equalisation reserve will draw £2.27m in 2026/27, a major in-year hit
findings.detail: After drawing only £0.67m during 2025/26, the council forecasts a material £2.27m draw in 2026/27 from its Business Rates Equalisation reserve. This is then topped up slightly (£0.20m per year) but never recovers to current levels. The pattern suggests business rates income is expected to be volatile and pressured in the near term.
findings.matters: Business rates are a volatile revenue stream. A large draw from this reserve signals the council is hedging against a sharp shortfall in 2026/27, which could indicate expected economic weakness or local property market stress.
findings.figures: Business Rates Equalisation: £2.405m (April 2025) → £1.740m (April 2026), then (2.265) 2026/27, 0.200 per year 2027–2030, ending at £3.205m
findings.quote: Business Rates Equalisation reserve: (2.405) opening, 0.665 transfer, (1.740) forecast closing, then (2.265) 2026/27, 0.200 2027/28, 0.200 2028/29, 0.200 2029/30, 0.200 2030/31, (3.205) expected balance

findings.headline: Market risk reserve growing to £13m suggests significant treasury or investment exposure
findings.detail: The Market Risk reserve is forecast to grow from £8.90m to £9.27m in 2025/26, then drawn at escalating rates (£0.59m to £1.00m per year). By 2031 it reaches £12.98m. This reserve exists to absorb unexpected financial volatility, suggesting the council has material exposure to markets (treasury, investments, or market-linked income).
findings.matters: A lender needs to know whether the council has treasury or market exposure that could crystallise losses, and whether reserve levels are adequate to absorb shocks without triggering borrowing.

findings.paper_title: UPDATED Appendix 3 - Section 25 Report of Chief Finance Officer
findings.headline: Transitional protection grant of £8.5m in 2028/29 is at risk of removal in 2029/30
findings.detail: The council benefits from £8.5m of transitional protection grant in 2028/29 as a buffer against the business rates reset and Fair Funding 2.0 changes. However, this protection ends after 2028/29, and there is no certainty beyond the current three-year spending review period (to March 2029). While the minister has stated the Government will look to avoid 'cliff-edges,' there is explicit risk this £8.5m is removed from 2029/30.
findings.matters: The £8.5m protection masks a deeper structural funding problem. If removed, it becomes an additional pressure on top of the already-identified £2.3m gap in 2027/28 and any further savings that have not been delivered. This creates potential for a cumulative funding shortfall of over £10m in 2029/30.
findings.figures: £8.5m transitional protection grant in 2028/29; no firm commitment beyond March 2029
findings.quote: There is a risk that the Government remove this funding in 2029/30, though the minister has said the Government will look to avoid "cliff-edges" in funding in the next spending review period.

findings.paper_title: UPDATED Appendix 3 - Section 25 Report of Chief Finance Officer
findings.headline: Contingency budget reduced, requiring services to identify mitigations with documented service impacts
findings.detail: The corporate contingency budget has been reduced for 2026/27 to £2.2m (5.5% of net budget). This means services projecting overspends must now develop written mitigation plans with explicit service impact statements, rather than drawing from a larger central buffer. The paper states services must 'identify mitigations along with service impacts for the Executive to consider.'
findings.matters: Reduced contingency limits the council's ability to absorb in-year pressures without service cuts or reserve drawdown. Combined with the declining savings delivery rate and rising overspends, this tightening creates higher refinancing risk if the council needs to draw on reserves.
findings.figures: £2.2m corporate contingency for 2026/27
findings.quote: As the value of the contingency budget has reduced for 2026/27, there is a greater need for services to identify mitigations along with service impacts for the Executive to consider whether they are prepared to implement the change

findings.paper_title: UPDATED Appendix 3 - Section 25 Report of Chief Finance Officer
findings.headline: Extreme dependency on business rates and council tax income, both in upper quartile risk
findings.detail: Business rates income represents 302.73% of baseline funding growth (6th highest retained growth of all councils), placing Cherwell in upper quartile risk. Council tax is 51.74% of net expenditure (upper quartile risk) due to nine years of no increases pre-2019. Both streams are volatile to economic and market conditions. The council holds a £9.3m market risk reserve and £5.9m interest rate equalisation reserve specifically for these risks.
findings.matters: The council's revenue model is heavily exposed to factors outside its control: business rates to economic growth and the Government's business rates reset decisions; council tax to property band growth and taxpayer resistance. A downturn in either stream creates immediate budget stress given the emerging 2027/28 gap.
findings.figures: Business rates growth ratio 302.73%; Council tax 51.74% of net revenue expenditure; £9.3m market risk reserve; £5.9m interest rate equalisation reserve held
findings.quote: This places the council at the upper end of risk, having the 6th highest retained growth of all councils. This is perceived as a risk as, in comparison with many other Districts, the council's retained income from business rates is high – which is a reflection of having a successful strategy to grow business rates in Cherwell

findings.paper_title: UPDATED Appendix 3 - Section 25 Report of Chief Finance Officer
findings.headline: Services forecast to overspend by £2.5m in 2025/26, masked by corporate underspend
findings.detail: The 2025/26 forecast as of December 2025 shows £2.499m in service overspends, only offset by £3.024m in corporate underspends, arriving at a balanced outturn. This pattern shows services are not controlling spend to budget. The paper introduces a 2% variance tolerance and Budget Oversight Group for services exceeding this threshold.
findings.matters: Services overspending and relying on central corporate reserves to balance is not a sustainable pattern. It signals weak individual budget control and means corporate reserves are being drawn down in-year rather than held for genuine emergency or investment.
findings.figures: £2.499m services overspend; £3.024m corporate underspends; £0.525m savings non-delivery
findings.quote: The council's forecast financial position as at the end of December 2025 shows a forecast outturn position of a balanced position. This is made up of £0.525m in-year savings non-delivery, £2.499m services overspend, offset by £3.024m corporate underspends.

findings.paper_title: UPDATED Appendix 3 - Section 25 Report of Chief Finance Officer
findings.headline: Debt:income ratio of 151% is extreme outlier — six times the district council median
findings.detail: Cherwell holds £165m gross external debt (forecast to fall to £149m by March 2026) against a median debt:income ratio of 9% for district councils. Cherwell's ratio is 151%. This reflects large capital schemes including Castle Quay and Graven Hill financed through borrowing. The council must refinance approximately £41m of maturing debt in 2026/27 at current market rates.
findings.matters: This leverage is extreme for a district council. While the paper claims borrowing costs are 'factored into the budget,' the refinancing risk is real: if interest rates fall more slowly than forecast (or rise), or if service income declines, debt serviceability becomes constrained. The council is also at the upper end of its Authorised Limit for External Debt.
findings.figures: £149m debt forecast March 2026; Cherwell debt:income 151% vs median 9%; ~£41m refinancing needed 2026/27; Authorised Limit £270m (down from £310m in 2025/26)
findings.quote: Cherwell at £165m and in the upper quartile of non-metropolitan district councils. This reflects the decisions taken to finance the capital programme, including Castle Quay and Graven Hill, through borrowing.

findings.paper_title: UPDATED Appendix 3 - Section 25 Report of Chief Finance Officer
findings.headline: Track record of delivering planned savings has deteriorated to 63-66%
findings.detail: Over six years, the council's savings delivery has declined: 80% in 2021/22, 75% in 2022/23, 80% in 2023/24, 63% in 2024/25, and 66% in 2025/26 (forecast). The paper acknowledges this pattern and states that 'where a service is overspending it should identify mitigations.' With £4.1m of savings required through 2030/31 and the emerging £2.3m gap, this deteriorating track record is material.
findings.matters: A lender cannot rely on a council to deliver cost reduction targets if two-thirds is the recent delivery rate. This limits the council's options for bridging the 2027/28 funding gap and increases refinancing risk.
findings.quote: The council identified a savings programme of £1.7m for 2024/25. The savings delivery was 63% with mitigations identified for non-delivery.

findings.paper_title: UPDATED Appendix 3 - Section 25 Report of Chief Finance Officer
findings.headline: Government settlement change in February 2026 created a £2.3m funding gap from 2027/28 onwards
findings.detail: The final local government finance settlement announced on 9 February 2026 reduced resources by £2.3m from 2027/28 compared to the provisional settlement announced 17 December 2025. The 2026/27 budget is balanced but there is now an identified £2.3m gap in 2027/28 with no funding solution yet identified. The paper states the council must 'identify how it intends to address' this gap.
findings.matters: This is a material structural deficit emerging just 12 months ahead. At £2.3m, it represents a significant portion of the council's discretionary spending. The council has a recent track record of delivering only 63-66% of identified savings targets, raising questions about its ability to close this gap through service reductions.
findings.figures: £2.3m annual reduction from 2027/28 onwards; gap identified for 2027/28, 2029/30, and 2030/31
findings.quote: The final settlement reduced the amount of resources the council will receive by £2.3m from 2027/28. The council now needs to deliver what is planned in the MTFS and identify how it intends to address the £2.3m gap in 2027/28.

findings.paper_title: UPDATED Appendix 3 - Section 25 Report of Chief Finance Officer
findings.headline: Auditor has disclaimed opinion on accounts for three consecutive years
findings.detail: Cherwell received a disclaimed audit opinion for 2022/23, 2023/24, and 2024/25. The paper notes this is a sector phenomenon but the impact is that auditors have not been able to certify the council's accounts. The auditors are developing a roadmap to return to standard opinions. However, the council did receive an unqualified value for money conclusion for both 2023/24 and 2024/25.
findings.matters: A disclaimed opinion means the auditor could not form any opinion on whether the accounts are materially correct. This is a significant governance red flag for external stakeholders and lenders assessing financial position, even if the VfM conclusion is positive.
findings.quote: As a result of receiving a disclaimed audit opinion in 2022/23, the council received a disclaimed opinion for its 2023/24 and 2024/25 accounts. These disclaimed opinions are as a result of the 2022/23 disclaimed opinion as the auditors ran out of time to get assurance over the opening balances

findings.headline: Significant environmental and decarbonisation capital programme spanning solar installations, electric heating, and net zero projects.
findings.detail: The council has allocated capital to multiple environmental priorities: solar PV at council properties (£0.708m Public Sector Decarbonisation Scheme, £0.028m Community Centre Solar Panels, £0.070m Spiceball Sports Centre, £0.135m Kidlington Sports Centre in pipeline), gas-to-electric heating replacements (£0.024m), vehicle replacement programmes (£4.265m), and pipeline net zero projects (£0.064m). Total Environmental Stewardship spending is £5.777m across five years.
findings.matters: Demonstrates capital commitments to net-zero transition and operating cost reduction, but signals medium-term revenue exposure if energy savings do not materialise as expected.
findings.figures: Environmental Stewardship total £5.777m; PSDS £0.940m; Vehicle Replacement £4.265m; solar/heating projects £0.227m

findings.headline: Disabled Facilities Grants programme (£8.1m total) contingent on Better Care Fund confirmation.
findings.detail: The £8.1m five-year Disabled Facilities Grants programme is fully externally financed and shows no net borrowing requirement, but is flagged as subject to confirmation of Better Care Fund allocation. If the Better Care Fund allocation is reduced or withdrawn, the council faces a funding gap for this statutory service.
findings.matters: Creates a funding risk for a statutory programme supporting vulnerable residents; non-delivery would either force revenue overspend or require capital scheme deferral.
findings.figures: £8.1m total grant funding dependent on Better Care Fund; annual commitments £1.944m (2026/27) and £1.539m (2027/28-2030/31)
findings.quote: Disabled Facilities Grants* Quality Housing and Place Making 1.944 1.539 1.539 1.539 1.539 8.100 (1.944) (1.539) (1.539) (1.539) (1.539) (8.100) - [with footnote] * Subject to confirmation of Better Care Fund allocation

findings.headline: Temporary accommodation acquisition strategy: £3m purchase plus £2m self-contained units in 2026/27.
findings.detail: The council is acquiring temporary accommodation stock rather than relying on private market placements, committing £3m to Purchase of Temporary Accommodation and £2m to Self-contained Temporary Accommodation Units in Bicester in year one alone. This is a strategic shift toward council-owned housing to manage temporary accommodation demand.
findings.matters: Signals housing pressure and a decision to capitalise rather than expense temporary housing. Creates ongoing management liabilities and indicates demand drivers that may constrain revenue budgets or asset values.
findings.figures: £3m for Purchase of Temporary Accommodation; £2m for Self-contained Temporary Accommodation Units – Bicester
findings.quote: Purchase of Temporary Accommodation Quality Housing and Place Making 3.000 - - - - 3.000 - - - - - - 3.000; Self contained Temporary Accommodation Units – Bicester Quality Housing and Place Making 2.000

findings.headline: Council Office Relocation commitment of £5.146m in 2027/28 with no parallel expenditure recorded.
findings.detail: The Council Office Relocation and Development project shows £5.146m in financing cash outflow in 2027/28 but no expenditure in the same year. This suggests either a multi-year project with deferred expenditure, a lease or PFI arrangement, or a strategic real estate decision with financing already committed.
findings.matters: A major strategic asset decision that signals long-term property strategy and creates a fixed cash commitment in year three; lenders assess whether this reflects planned growth, cost-saving, or estate consolidation.
findings.figures: £5.146m financing outflow in 2027/28
findings.quote: Council Office Relocation and Development Running the Business - - - - - - - (5.146) - - - (5.146) (5.146)

findings.headline: Five-year borrowing requirement of £8.495m, front-loaded in 2026/27.
findings.detail: The capital programme requires £8.495m in borrowing across five years. The heaviest borrowing demand is in year one (£4.245m for Community Leadership, £5.146m for Running the Business across its programmes). Borrowing then declines sharply to £1.539m or less in subsequent years.
findings.matters: A material borrowing decision affecting debt capacity and treasury management; front-loading in year one requires close attention to cash flow and debt sustainability.
findings.figures: Total borrowing £8.495m; 2026/27 borrowing £8.264m; 2027/28 £10.178m (but includes Council Office financing); 2028/29-2030/31 combined £4.617m

findings.headline: Property portfolio is illiquid and cannot be quickly converted to cash in stressed market conditions, limiting ability to refinance debt
findings.detail: The council holds major property assets in retail (Castle Quay, Pioneer Square) and industrial/warehouse (Tramway Industrial Estate) sectors. The strategy acknowledges that 'property is relatively difficult to sell to convert to cash at short notice and can take a considerable period to sell in certain market conditions.' The council recognises 'illiquidity as a risk in property' and notes that whilst the portfolio is uncharged (not pledged as collateral), this 'can expose an owner to greater risk of selling an illiquid asset at an inopportune time' if borrowing becomes unavailable.
findings.matters: If PWLB refinancing became constrained (as it was during COVID), the council might need to liquidate property to repay debt. Selling illiquid retail properties in a weak market would likely require steep discounts, crystallising losses and further eroding the CFR-to-asset cushion.
findings.figures: Castle Quay Centre and Waterfront (Banbury), Pioneer Square (Bicester), Tramway Industrial Estate (Banbury) are the largest strategic assets. Current book value of these four assets: £50.9m.
findings.quote: property is relatively difficult to sell to convert to cash at short notice and can take a considerable period to sell in certain market conditions.

findings.headline: £5m capital investment in temporary accommodation in 2026/27 signals housing pressure or homelessness crisis management
findings.detail: The council is proposing £3m for purchase of temporary accommodation units and £2m for self-contained temporary accommodation units in Bicester, totalling £5m of the £8.5m capital additions for 2026/27. This suggests either statutory homelessness duty pressures or a deliberate strategy to manage accommodation costs. Such spending indicates underlying demand pressures in the housing/homelessness space that are not being met by existing supply.
findings.matters: Temporary accommodation purchases often indicate that service demand (homelessness) is outpacing supply or that existing temporary accommodation spend (usually revenue) is becoming unaffordable, requiring capitalisation. This can be a leading indicator of broader social pressure and future budget stress.
findings.figures: Purchase of Temporary Accommodation: £3.0m (2026/27). Self-contained Temporary Accommodation Units: £2.0m (2026/27). Total capital additions 2026/27: £8.5m. Whitelands Farm 3G Pitch: £0.9m.
findings.quote: Purchase of Temporary Accommodation 3.0 - Self-contained Temporary Accommodation Units – Bicester 2.0

findings.headline: Capital Financing Requirement increasing to £238.8m in 2026/27, with CFR now 84% of the council's long-term asset base
findings.detail: The council's CFR (the amount of capital expenditure not yet permanently financed) is forecast to rise from £233.9m in 2025/26 to £238.8m in 2026/27 before declining. More concerning, the ratio of CFR to long-term assets is now 84%, meaning the council's debt is equivalent to 84% of its total capital asset value. This ratio has climbed from 75% in 2020/21, a four-year deterioration. The council projects CFR clearance by 2066 'mainly due to the annual minimum revenue provision' but that is 40 years away.
findings.matters: A rising CFR-to-asset ratio signals that the council is borrowing closer to the limit of its asset base. If further asset valuations fall (as property has done), the cushion shrinks further. A lender wants to see headroom here; at 84%, there is little.
findings.quote: As of 31st March 2025, the Council's CFR amounted to 84 percent of the value of its total capital worth (Long-term asset value), demonstrating that the Council's total capital worth exceeds its borrowing requirement.

findings.headline: Council holds £57m in loans to subsidiaries (Graven Hill, Crown House) with £17m in undrawn commitments and credit loss allowance of £0.7m
findings.detail: The council has advanced £57.2m in loans to subsidiaries, has a loss allowance of £0.7m (indicating recognised credit risk), and is contractually committed to lend a further £17m to Graven Hill. The council notes it recognizes 'loss allowance for loans, reflecting the likelihood of non-payment' and that subsidiaries are assessed individually through full business cases. Repayment depends on the subsidiaries' performance in property development and residential letting markets.
findings.matters: Subsidiary loan defaults would immediately impact the council's cash position and would likely trigger additional MRP charges if loan valuations had to be written down further, creating a direct hit to revenue. The undrawn £17m commitment is a contingent liability that could be drawn if the subsidiary faces construction overruns or market headwinds.
findings.figures: Service loans to subsidiaries: £56.6m gross, £0.6m loss allowance, £56.0m net (2024/25). Commitments to lend: £17.0m to Graven Hill (revolving credit facility to 2026). Bonds and guarantees: £1.4m in place, £10.3m agreed in principle.
findings.quote: Accounting standards (IFRS 9) require the council to set aside loss allowance for loans, reflecting the likelihood of non-payment.

findings.headline: Council's affordability critically depends on income from stressed property holdings that generated only 0.9% return in 2024/25
findings.detail: Service investment income (primarily rental income from properties and loan interest from subsidiaries) represents 29-32% of the council's net revenue stream. This income is essential to offset financing costs; without it, the net financing burden would be unsustainable. However, property investments returned only 0.9% in 2024/25 and are forecast at 0.1% in 2025/26. The document acknowledges the risk explicitly: 'Investment income represents a significant proportion of the net revenue stream and therefore the risks around loss of this income should be monitored closely.'
findings.matters: If tenant default, void rates, or further valuations losses impact rental income, the council could face sudden revenue shortfalls. The council is already operating on a knife edge: the affordability ratio (financing costs minus investment income) is -1.0% for 2026/27 but turns positive (0.9%) by 2028/29, meaning costs start to exceed income.
findings.quote: Investment income represents a significant proportion of the net revenue stream and therefore the risks around loss of this income should be monitored closely.

findings.headline: Strategic property assets have lost £106m in book value, with town-centre retail portfolio under sustained pressure
findings.detail: Four major property investments show cumulative book losses of £106m from their original investment cost. Castle Quay Waterfront lost £45.8m (from £68.6m invested), Castle Quay Shopping Centre lost £56.9m (from £64.7m invested), and Pioneer Square lost £2.9m (from £8.2m invested). The document attributes this to 'the changing nature of town centres and the retail market nationwide' and flags over-exposure to town centre retailing as a specific risk.
findings.matters: A lender's security position depends on asset valuations. Sustained property losses in retail signal either that the council paid too much, market fundamentals have shifted unfavourably, or both. The trend suggests further pressure is possible.
findings.figures: Castle Quay Waterfront: investment £68.6m, book value £22.8m (loss £45.8m); Castle Quay Shopping Centre: investment £64.7m, book value £13.6m (loss £56.9m); Tramway Industrial Estate: investment £9.6m, book value £9.2m; Pioneer Square: investment £8.2m, book value £5.3m (loss £2.9m)
findings.quote: The decline in book values have been driven by multiple factors, particularly the changing nature of town centres and the retail market nationwide.

findings.headline: Financing cost ratio rising to nearly 32% of revenue by 2028/29, driven by declining government grants
findings.detail: The council's ratio of financing costs (interest and MRP) to net revenue stream is forecast to reach 31.9% by 2028/29, up from 28.3% in 2024/25. The document explicitly states 'This indicator shows that the ratio of financing costs to net revenue streams is high and increasing across the MTFS, which is primarily due to the forecast in reduction in revenue resources.' This ratio is trending sharply upward over the five-year forecast.
findings.matters: A lender needs to see headroom in a council's budget for debt service; 32% is at the upper end of prudent levels and leaves little buffer for revenue pressures or service demand shocks.
findings.quote: This indicator shows that the ratio of financing costs to net revenue streams is high and increasing across the MTFS, which is primarily due to the forecast in reduction in revenue resources.

findings.headline: Debt rescheduling opportunity rejected due to higher refinancing costs outweighing discount
findings.detail: PWLB offered a £9.4m discount for early repayment of the council's loans, but refinancing at current market rates (4.45%) exceeds the council's average loan rate of 2.34% by a substantial margin. After amortising the discount over ten years, the net effect would be a £924,383 annual revenue cost—making the opportunity economically unfeasible.
findings.matters: The council's inability to execute debt restructuring despite a material discount reflects the structural cost of rising refinancing rates. This constrains the council's financial management options and signals higher debt servicing costs ahead.
findings.figures: Available discount: £9,373,131; Amortised annual discount: £937,313; Increased annual interest cost at 4.45%: £1,861,695; Net annual revenue burden: £924,383; Council's average loan rate: 2.34%
findings.quote: In September 2025 the PWLB was offering a discount of £9,373,131 for the early repayment of all the loans made to the council that have over 12 months left to maturity... Currently the PWLB 1 year rate is 4.45% which would mean an increased interest payments of £1,861,695 annually, reduced by the £937,313 amortised discount, would be an increased revenue burden of £924,383.

findings.headline: Investment cash portfolio declining alongside rising refinancing costs
findings.detail: The council's liquid investment portfolio is forecast to fall from £26m in 2025/26 to £23m in 2026/27, reducing expected investment income from £0.886m to £0.826m. This contraction occurs as the council finances its capital programme through internal borrowing—drawing down reserves rather than accessing external debt.
findings.matters: Shrinking cash reserves combined with lower investment income reduces the council's financial flexibility and its ability to self-finance capital projects or absorb unexpected costs.
findings.figures: Investment portfolio: £26m (2025/26) to £23m (2026/27); Investment income: £0.886m (2025/26 budget) to £0.826m (2026/27 budget); Average interest rate: 3.38% to 3.54%
findings.quote: The budget for treasury investment income in 2026/27 is £0.826m, based on an average investment portfolio of £23m at an average interest rate of 3.54%. This is a slight decrease from the £0.886m budgeted for in 2025/26, based on an average investment portfolio of £26m

findings.headline: Capital reserves forecast to decline by 72% in a single year
findings.detail: Capital reserves are projected to fall from £4.7m in 2025/26 to £1.3m in 2026/27, a loss of £3.4m. This sharp depletion represents a significant erosion of the council's capital resource buffer in just twelve months, with reserves remaining at that low level in subsequent forecasts.
findings.matters: A rapid drawdown of capital reserves signals either heavy capital spending or a deteriorating liquidity position. Either indicates reduced financial resilience and capacity to absorb future shocks.
findings.figures: Capital Reserves: £5.3m (2024/25 actual), £4.7m (2025/26 forecast), £1.3m (2026/27 forecast), £1.2m (2027/28 forecast), £1.2m (2028/29 forecast)

news_drafts.headline: Significant concentration of borrowing due within 12 months requires refinancing
news_drafts.lead: Concentration of near-term maturities creates refinancing risk; if rates rise while the council refinances £36m, borrowing costs could increase materially from the current 2.87% average.

news_drafts.headline: Council relying on one-time PWLB early redemption discount to boost reserves
news_drafts.lead: Using a non-recurring windfall to boost reserves creates false impression of financial strength and makes budget balancing more difficult in future years.

news_drafts.headline: Crown House loan revalued downward due to non-market interest rate
news_drafts.lead: Loans at non-market rates suggest capital misallocation or subsidies; the IFRS9 revaluation indicates overvaluation of the investment or risk in the underlying company.
